1.title: The Skeleton Song and Dance
1.caption: An 1897 vaudeville theatrical poster for Bimbo of Bombay, a musical comedy directed by Ed M. Graves. Along the bottom, four dancing skeletons advertise a performance titled The Skeleton Song and Dance, illustrating the popularity of animated death imagery in theatrical entertainment decades before Disney's The Skeleton Dance (1929).
1.credit: H. C. Miner Litho. Co., A Magical Musical Comedy, Bimbo of Bombay, 1897. Lithograph. Library of Congress, Theatrical Poster Collection. U.S. public domain; no known restrictions on publication.

2.title: The Cemetery of the Holy Innocents
2.caption: Fédor Hoffbauer's nineteenth-century reconstruction of the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents in Paris, depicting its appearance around 1750. Along the left, the covered charnel-house galleries recall a burial landscape in which the remains of the dead were stored above the activities of the living. The celebrated Danse Macabre of 1424–25 had occupied another gallery, the Charnier des Lingères, before its destruction in the seventeenth century.
2.credit: Fédor Hoffbauer, Le Cimetière des Innocents en 1750, published in Paris à travers les âges (1875–1882), Plate II. Lithograph by A. Bayalos. Original drawing held by Musée Carnavalet, Paris, inv. D.7922.  (CC0).

3.title: A Portable Procession
3.caption: A page from Guy Marchant's La Danse macabre nouvelle, published in Paris in 1486. Marchant's illustrated editions helped transform the monumental Dance of Death associated with the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents into a portable printed work, allowing its imagery and verses to circulate beyond the cemetery walls.
3.credit: Guy Marchant, La Danse macabre nouvelle (Paris, 1486). Bibliothèque nationale de France, Réserve des livres rares, Rés. Ye-189. Digitized by Gallica, BnF. View original. Source: https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b2200008n/f2.item?__cf_chl_tk=Shkml2IT013Em4F1Eg7MLO01RL6 p8_tfbH1FjDFR7AA-1793395713-1.0.1.1-L0dKTk6aP617e5b_FPnKhca_7518J07t0kMQ3ISuxCE#

4.title: Before the Dead Danced
4.caption: Three richly dressed kings confront three decomposing corpses in an illuminated manuscript dating to approximately 1310. The encounter, known as The Three Living and the Three Dead, warned that worldly splendour could offer no protection against bodily decay. Predating the Black Death, it provides evidence of the religious and visual traditions of mortality that existed before the monumental Danse Macabre of fifteenth-century Paris.
4.credit: The Three Living and the Three Dead, Psalter of Robert de Lisle, c. 1310. British Library, Arundel MS 83, fol. 127r. Image reproduction rights to be confirmed for the selected digital file. Specific photo in use from: https://www.facsimilefinder.com/articles/de-lisle-psalter-facsimile-alumina/

5.title: Two Encounters
5.caption: Two encounters from a Parisian Book of Hours, produced around 1430–1435. Left: A probable knight, wearing a chaperon hat with a badge, a gold collar, a sheathed sword, and spurs, stands with his arms extended as two skeletal figures grasp him on either side. The scene occupies a marginal medallion surrounded by elaborate foliage and vinescroll ornament. Right: A probable magistrate, distinguished by his long robes and hat, is similarly confronted by two skeletal figures. Although their clothing and attributes proclaim different positions within medieval society, neither can escape the summons of the dead.
5.credit: Left: Dance of Death: Knight (?), Book of Hours, Paris, c. 1430–1435. Illuminated manuscript, MS M.359, fol. 129v. The Morgan Library & Museum, New York. Collection record. Right: Dance of Death: Magistrate (?), Book of Hours, Paris, c. 1430–1435. Illuminated manuscript, MS M.359, fol. 128r. The Morgan Library & Museum, New York. Collection record. Source: Folio 129v https://ica.themorgan.org/manuscript/page/255/76807; folio 128r https://ica.themorgan.org/manuscript/page/252/76807 Explore full manuscript: https://ica.themorgan.org/manuscript/page/1/76807

6.title: Society and Death
6.caption: Ecclesiastical dignitaries, secular rulers, and other richly dressed figures join skeletal partners in this sixteenth-century German interpretation of the Dance of Death. Although the participants share a common fate, their clothing, attributes, and positions preserve the distinctions of the society they represent. The contrast between the animated skeletons and their living companions makes the procession's central paradox immediately visible: death comes for everyone, but the living are never quite anonymous.
6.credit: Anonymous German artist, The Dance of Death, sixteenth century. Pen and brown ink, brush and brown ink, watercolor, gouache, and gold paint. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, accession no. 1996.70. Public Domain. .

7.title: The Papal Legate and the Duke
7.caption: Guy Marchant’s printed Dance of Death pairs the papal legate and the duke with skeletal companions. The supplied image is labelled “Le legat” and “Le duc”.
7.credit: Guy Marchant, Dance of Death, papal legate and duke. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The supplied draft’s women’s Dance caption does not describe this image; final caption and edition require editorial review.

8.title: Two Dances, Two Churches
8.caption: Painted in 1474, the Dance of Death at Beram transforms the inevitability of mortality into an animated and occasionally irreverent spectacle. Skeletons play music, gesture toward their living companions, and lead representatives of society toward an enthroned Death. Among the participants are figures who attempt to purchase their release, including a pope, queen, and merchant or moneylender. The fresco exposes the futility of wealth and status through gestures that are at once theatrical and unmistakably moralizing.
8.credit: Vincent of Kastav, Dance of Death, 1474. Fresco, Church of St Mary on Škriline, Beram, Croatia. Photograph: Toffel, 2008, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

9.title: The Nuremberg Chronicle
9.caption: Skeletons join in a lively dance in this woodcut from the Nuremberg Chronicle, published in 1493. Their animated gestures demonstrate how the imagery of death could combine theatrical movement with the contemplation of mortality. Within a generation, Hans Holbein the Younger would transform the tradition further, placing Death directly into the everyday activities of the living.
9.credit: Michael Wolgemut, Dance of Death, leaf from The Nuremberg Chronicle, 1493. Woodcut and letterpress text. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Bequest of Herbert Mitchell, 2008 (2018.839.160). Public Domain. Source: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/390220

10.title: The Price of Possession
10.caption: A wealthy man yells as Death reaches for the coins piled upon his table. Chests and money bags crowd the foreground, surrounding him with the possessions he can no longer protect. In Holbein's Dance of Death, the familiar medieval procession gives way to individual encounters, exposing the fragility of wealth and worldly security.
10.credit: Hans Holbein the Younger (designer), Dance of Death: The Miser, c. 1526. Woodcut, engraved by Hans Lützelburger. Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland, accession no. 1929.161. Image: Cleveland Museum of Art, Open Access, CC0 (public domain). Source: https://www.clevelandart.org/art/1929.161

11.title: The Unfinished Dance
11.caption: Thirteen figures remain from a monumental Dance of Death painted in the late fifteenth century. A preacher introduces a procession of skeletal figures and representatives of earthly authority, accompanied by dialogue in Low German. The surviving canvas extends approximately 7.5 metres, but the original composition was probably considerably longer. Its abrupt ending offers a reminder of how much of the medieval Dance of Death has disappeared and how carefully its surviving evidence must be interpreted.
11.credit: Workshop of Bernt Notke, Dance of Death (Surmatants), late fifteenth century. Oil and tempera on canvas, 163 × 750 cm. Art Museum of Estonia, Niguliste Museum, Tallinn, accession no. EKM j 18761 N 153.  Source: BerntNotke, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

12.title: The Living Before the Dead
12.caption: The surviving Dance of Death displayed in St Anthony's Chapel of the Niguliste Museum, Tallinn. Centuries after its creation, the monumental painting continues to confront visitors with a procession whose original extent, location, and audience remain incompletely understood. Its medieval spectators have disappeared, but the encounter between the living and the painted dead continues.
12.credit: Attributed to the workshop of Bernt Notke, Dance of Death, late fifteenth century. Art Museum of Estonia, Niguliste Museum, Tallinn. Source: https://nigulistemuuseum.ekm.ee/en/dance-of-death/

hrastovlje.caption: Completed in 1490, the Dance of Death at Hrastovlje leads representatives of different social ranks and stages of life toward a common destination. Popes and rulers share the procession with those possessing far less earthly authority. Set within a larger programme of Christian imagery, the fresco demonstrates how the familiar medieval warning about mortality could acquire a distinctive visual character in a different community and religious setting.
hrastovlje.credit: John of Kastav, Dance of Death, 1490. Fresco, Church of the Holy Trinity, Hrastovlje, Slovenia. Photograph: János Korom Dr., 2009, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
